posts.topic: Cassandra to ScyllaDB migration (trillions of messages)
posts.hook: They used fewer nodes, not more, to handle more load
posts.opening_style: rhetorical question (Ever wonder how Discord stores...)
posts.key_numbers: 177 → 72 nodes, p99 read 40-125ms → 15ms, p99 write 5-70ms → 5ms
posts.lesson: Your database's ceiling is often the runtime beneath it, not the database design

posts.topic: Pod architecture — isolated data cells instead of microservices
posts.hook: Monolith survives Black Friday by isolating state, not splitting services
posts.key_numbers: BFCM 2024: 1.19T edge requests, 10.5T DB queries, 284M req/min peak. BFCM 2025: 14.8T DB queries, 489M req/min peak.
posts.lesson: Scaling compute and limiting blast radius are two different problems. Isolate state, keep the app simple.

posts.topic: Multiplayer editing — rejected OT in favor of last-writer-wins per property
posts.hook: Rejected the industry-standard algorithm (OT) because design isn't text
posts.opening_style: rhetorical question (Ever wonder how Figma lets 30 people...)
posts.key_numbers: Map<ObjectID, Map<Property, Value>> data model. Server tracks latest value per property. 2025 added Eg-walker for code editing specifically.
posts.lesson: Industry standard is contextual. Understand your problem's shape before picking an algorithm.

posts.topic: Workers run on V8 isolates, not containers — 100x faster cold starts
posts.hook: Rejected containers as the isolation primitive and rebuilt serverless around V8
posts.opening_style: shared-pain-point opener (Every serverless platform has the same problem: cold starts.)
posts.key_numbers: Cold start under 5ms (vs 200ms-1s+ for containers). 40% of Lambda cold starts exceed 500ms (Datadog 2024). 10-100x less memory than containers. Thousands of isolates per process.
posts.lesson: The default infrastructure primitive is a choice. Ask what it's protecting you from, and whether you need that protection.

posts.topic: Sharding Postgres monolith — 480 logical shards, workspace ID partition key, then re-sharding 32→96 physical DBs
posts.hook: Monolith lasted 5 years and 4 orders of magnitude. Then VACUUM stopped working.
posts.key_numbers: 480 logical shards, 32→96 physical DBs, 20B→200B blocks in 3 years, 96-CPU migration machine, 5 min downtime, TXID wraparound at 4B
posts.lesson: Shard before your database is so strained that the migration itself becomes dangerous.

posts.topic: Sharding IDs — 64-bit self-routing IDs using PL/pgSQL inside Postgres, rejected Snowflake/UUID/ticket servers
posts.hook: Rejected every existing ID solution. Wrote a Postgres function instead.
posts.key_numbers: 41 bits timestamp + 13 bits shard + 10 bits sequence = 64 bits. 1024 IDs/shard/ms. 8192 logical shards max.
posts.lesson: Same concept as Snowflake but inside the database. Best architecture for a small team is the one you can debug at 3am.

posts.topic: DOMA — Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture, organizing 2200 services into 70 domains with gateways and layers
posts.hook: Microservices are supposed to make teams faster. Uber had 2,200 and they were slowing teams down.
posts.key_numbers: 2200 services → 70 domains. Half-life 1.5 years. 50 services across 12 teams for 1 bug. Integration time 3 days → 3 hours. Onboarding reduced 25-50%.
posts.lesson: The organizing principle above microservices matters more than the microservices themselves.

posts.topic: EVCache evolution from RAM to SSD — Moneta (RocksDB) then extstore, trillions of ops/day
posts.hook: Netflix calls EVCache the hidden microservice. Then the cost of keeping it all in RAM arrived.
posts.key_numbers: Petabytes, hundreds of billions items, trillions ops/day. RAM <1μs, SSD 100-500μs, SLA 1ms. Moneta: 60% cluster reduction. r3 80GB → i2 800GB (10x storage).
posts.lesson: The real question is not RAM or disk — it is what latency does your SLA actually require.

posts.topic: Idempotency keys — 3 failure modes, UUID per request, cached response, 24hr expiry, 500 edge case
posts.hook: A request fails in 3 ways and only one is obvious — the third is the dangerous one.
posts.key_numbers: 3 failure modes. Same key + diff params = 400. Keys expire 24hrs. Exponential backoff + jitter. 500 + payment network = roll forward.
posts.lesson: Retry logic is the contract. In a distributed system, did this request succeed is never a simple question.

posts.topic: Kafka origin — M×N pipeline problem, distributed commit log, 1B to 7T messages/day, internal release branch
posts.hook: In 2010, LinkedIn had a data problem existing tools could not solve — so they built Kafka.
posts.key_numbers: 1B/day (2011) → 20B (2012) → 200B (2013) → 1T/4.5M sec peak (2014) → 7T/day today. 100+ clusters, 4000+ brokers, 100K topics, 7M partitions.
posts.lesson: The log is a more fundamental abstraction than most engineers realize. Pull model + persistence + partitioning generalizes to every organization generating continuous event data.

posts.topic: Replaced Elasticsearch with Apache Lucene-based in-house search engine — segment replication, indexer/searcher split
posts.hook: Elasticsearch is the default. DoorDash replaced it with what Elasticsearch is built on.
posts.key_numbers: p99.9 latency -50%, hardware costs -75%. Shard replication → segment replication via S3. Indexer + Searcher scale independently.
posts.lesson: The tool you outgrow made assumptions that stopped fitting your workload. Going down one abstraction layer and building to fit is sometimes cheaper than fighting the default.

posts.topic: CRISP — critical path analysis for microservices, finds actual bottleneck vs slowest service
posts.hook: 40K endpoints. When a request is slow, which service do you fix? Not the slowest one.
posts.key_numbers: 40K endpoints, 100M daily users, 1500-11K spans per trace, 100K+ traces analyzed, 10x diurnal difference found.
posts.lesson: Critical path contribution and individual latency are different metrics. Only one predicts whether your optimization changes the user experience.

posts.topic: MySQL Raft — Raft consensus built into MySQL, binlog as Raft log, leadership inside mysqld
posts.hook: One of the largest MySQL deployments. Safety enforced by scripts, not protocol. Until now.
posts.key_numbers: Millions of shards, petabytes. Thousands of injected failovers in testing. One membership change at a time. Majority quorum required for commit.
posts.lesson: When you maintain consistency between two separate systems, ask whether one can own the state both depend on. The coordination problem disappears.

posts.topic: Chaos Monkey and the Simian Army — intentionally killing production instances to build resilience
posts.hook: 2010. Netflix finishes migrating to AWS. Every instance can be terminated at any time. What do you do?
posts.key_numbers: 65,000 instances terminated in year 1. Runs 9am-3pm weekdays only. Chaos Monkey 2010, Simian Army 2011, open-sourced 2012.
posts.lesson: The value is not the tool. It is the mindset shift: from assuming systems will be up to designing so their failure is invisible.

posts.topic: Dynein — Resque to Quartz+MySQL to SQS+DynamoDB. Query amplification was the bottleneck.
posts.hook: Resque was at-most-once. That was the problem Airbnb couldn't ignore.
posts.key_numbers: Quartz: 1K QPS max on r4.8xlarge, 1 enqueue = 4 SELECTs + 3 INSERTs. DynamoDB: 1 enqueue = 1 WCU PUT, 1 dequeue = 2 WCU + 1 RCU, <1/3 cost. p95 timing < 10 seconds.
posts.lesson: Choose infrastructure based on your actual requirements. Resque was right for the monolith. SQS+DynamoDB was right for services. The tool changed because the architecture changed.

posts.topic: Kafka Dead Letter Queues — non-blocking reprocessing via retry topic cascade, leaky bucket delay, DLQ merge
posts.hook: Every Kafka tutorial says retry inline. At scale this blocks the partition. Wrong mental model.
posts.key_numbers: Driver Injury Protection: 200+ cities. Retry topics: configurable delays per level. Consumer Proxy: onboarded hundreds of services. DLQ ops: list, purge, merge.
posts.lesson: Separate the fast path from the slow path. Primary consumer must never be blocked by failure recovery. Retry happens on its own timeline.

posts.topic: S3 US-EAST-1 outage — mistyped capacity-removal command, index + placement subsystem full restart, status dashboard hosted on S3 itself
posts.hook: A routine billing-debug playbook command, one wrong input, and AWS's own status page couldn't load because it was hosted on the S3 that had just gone dark
posts.key_numbers: 9:37 AM PST start, ~4 hours total outage, ~2 hours before status dashboard could update, ~$150M in S&P 500 losses (Cyence estimate)
posts.lesson: The failure mode that mattered wasn't in the code. It was in a system so reliable that no one had rehearsed what a full restart of its core subsystems would actually cost.

posts.topic: Earlybird real-time search — MySQL to custom Lucene rewrite in 2010, then unrolled linked lists to skip lists in 2020 to fix 15-second indexing lag
posts.hook: A decade after Twitter first solved 'real-time' search, a new tweet could still take up to 15 seconds to become searchable — because the fix from 2010 had its own aging assumption baked in
posts.key_numbers: ~6,000 tweets/sec ingested (~500M/day), 2B+ queries/day at ~50ms avg latency, 17K QPS on a 16M-tweet segment, 15s indexing lag in 2019 cut to ~1s (>90% reduction) via skip lists in 2020
posts.lesson: The system built to escape one era's staleness spent the next decade quietly becoming the source of the next one — 'real-time' isn't a fixed target.

posts.topic: Elixir at 5M concurrent users — Manifold batches cross-node sends by remote node instead of looping send/2 per PID, and the consistent-hash ring rewritten into pure Elixir + ETS to remove a single-owner-process bottleneck
posts.hook: Distributed Erlang makes a remote send/2 look identical in code to a local one — Discord found out that at 100,000 PIDs per guild process, 'looks the same' and 'costs the same' are different claims
posts.key_numbers: Up to 30K concurrent users in one guild (r/Overwatch), ~100K session PIDs on busy guild processes, ~70µs per remote send/2, packets/sec -50% immediately after Manifold, ring lookup ~12µs each, ~30s aggregate lookup cost during a mass-reconnect storm
posts.lesson: Location transparency didn't get removed by either fix — Discord just stopped paying its cost by accident, once per PID, and started paying it on purpose, once per node.

posts.topic: Manual MySQL sharding — rejected auto-clustering (Cassandra/Membase) after a rebalancing bug lost ~20% of data, rebuilt on deterministic 64-bit IDs (16-bit shard + 10-bit type + 36-bit local) with no auto-failover, ever
posts.hook: A rebalancing bug flipped a secondary to primary mid-transfer and cost Pinterest ~20% of its data — so they threw out automatic clustering and wrote a sharding function by hand instead
posts.key_numbers: Jan 2012: 11.7M monthly users, 6 engineers. Oct 2012: ~22M monthly users, 40 engineers, 88 sharded MySQL boxes. 64-bit ID = 16-bit shard + 10-bit type + 36-bit local. 4,096 shards live at launch of 65,536 possible. ~20% data lost in the rebalancing failure that triggered the rewrite.
posts.lesson: Automation isn't the goal. A failure mode you can actually reason about at 3am is — Pinterest traded invisible auto-rebalancing for a slower, manual, human-owned failover.

posts.topic: October 4, 2021 global outage — an audit-tool bug let a routine backbone-capacity command withdraw every BGP route, and Facebook's own DNS servers correctly self-withdrew their advertisements when they lost the backbone, which then broke the internal recovery tools and the badge readers on data center doors, all of which ran on the same network
posts.hook: A safety mechanism designed to make DNS servers withdraw themselves when unhealthy worked exactly as intended — and that correctness is what took Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp off the internet for six hours, then locked the engineers who could fix it out of the building
posts.key_numbers: 15:39 UTC command run, BGP restored ~21:50 UTC, DNS ~22:05 UTC, full service ~23:00 UTC (~6-7 hrs total), ~3.5B people affected across the app family, ~$60-100M estimated lost revenue for the day, Meta stock closed down ~4.9%
posts.lesson: The tradeoffs don't disappear when you add a safety mechanism. They just move — usually into the one scenario nobody modeled: everything failing at once.

posts.topic: July 2019 global outage — a WAF refactor meant to cut CPU use quietly deleted the circuit breaker for runaway regexes; three weeks later a routine rule with a nested-wildcard regex pinned CPU near 100% worldwide, and the fix was the same instant-global-push mechanism that caused it
posts.hook: One misconfigured regex, 100% CPU across the entire global network, and a 27-minute wait to reach for a kill switch nobody had planned to use against themselves
posts.key_numbers: 13:42 UTC deploy, 13:45 UTC first page (CPU near 100% worldwide), 14:02 UTC root cause isolated, 14:09 UTC recovered — 27 minutes total. CPU protection removed 3 weeks earlier during a WAF refactor. ~3,868 WAF Managed Rules hand-audited afterward.
posts.lesson: They kept the tool that pushes a fix everywhere in seconds. They just made sure it could no longer push an unbounded bug everywhere in seconds without anyone noticing first.

posts.topic: Storage Pods (2009) — built a $7,867 4U box of 45 consumer SATA drives instead of buying an EMC SAN/NetApp filer/Amazon S3, solved chassis vibration by pinning drives rigid instead of cushioning them, then in 2013 tested a full pod of 'enterprise' drives against the consumer fleet and found the enterprise drives failed more often
posts.hook: Backblaze tested the 'pay for enterprise storage' assumption twice — once on the hardware, once on the drives — and the enterprise option lost both times
posts.key_numbers: Sept 2009: 67TB, 45 consumer SATA drives, $7,867 material cost, ~$0.11/GB, ~1/10th the all-in cost of EMC/NetApp/Dell/S3. Pod 5.0: $0.044/GB. Pod 6.0 (60 drives, 480TB, one 4U box): $0.036/GB. 2013 experiment: one full pod of enterprise drives had a higher failure rate than the consumer fleet.
posts.lesson: We default to paying for the enterprise label because verifying it ourselves feels like too much work. Backblaze ran the numbers instead of assuming them — on the box, then on the drives — and cheaper won both times.

posts.topic: Iguazu event platform — consolidated one-off SQS/Kinesis pipelines per event type onto a single Kafka+Flink platform (HTTP Kafka proxy extended from Confluent's OSS version, Flink fan-out to Snowflake/Redis/Chronosphere, Protobuf schemas validated in CI), cutting latency to Snowflake from a day to minutes at hundreds of billions of events/day — then found onboarding a new event source was still gated by a GitHub-PR-plus-Atlantis-plus-Terraform chain requiring manual on-call approval by email, and replaced it with a self-service API
posts.hook: DoorDash's event platform moves hundreds of billions of events a day at 99.99% reliability. Its bottleneck for years wasn't Kafka throughput — it was an on-call engineer's inbox
posts.key_numbers: Latency to Snowflake: up to 1 day → a few minutes. Hundreds of billions of events/day, 99.99% delivery. Topic onboarding: ~48hr guarantee → under 1hr (often ~15 min), a 95% reduction. On-call load: -4hrs/week. ~100 topics self-served/week. Product-launch PR queues could exceed 20/hour under the old process.
posts.lesson: The part of a system engineers spend the most time optimizing is rarely the part that's actually slowing it down. A platform tuned to move hundreds of billions of events a day was throttled by a pull request waiting on a human.

posts.topic: Envoy origin story — built as a language-agnostic sidecar proxy to replace a mishmash of per-language client libraries (PHP, Python) and an ELB/CloudWatch layer that couldn't report p50/p99 latency, so a struggling downstream degraded via capped concurrent retries and circuit breaking instead of triggering a retry-storm cascading failure
posts.hook: By 2015, Lyft had about 30 microservices — not a lot — and its own engineers were already wary of putting a single service call in a critical path. Not because the services were slow. Because when a call failed, nobody could say why
posts.key_numbers: ~30 microservices when Matt Klein joined Lyft (May 2015). By Sept 2016 open-source launch: 100+ services meshed, millions of req/sec. By Sept 2017 CNCF donation: thousands of nodes, 2M+ req/sec, every system at Lyft. Envoy graduated CNCF Nov 2018; later adopted as the data plane under Istio and AWS App Mesh.
posts.lesson: The sidecar didn't make the network simple — it added a proxy hop to every call. It moved the complexity somewhere everyone could see, instrument once, and fix in one place, instead of copy-pasted into thirty different client libraries.

posts.topic: July 2019 core banking outage caused by a misconfigured Cassandra auto_bootstrap flag — new nodes added during a routine scale-up took over their assigned token ranges immediately, before streaming the underlying data in, so queries against those ranges returned wrong balances and missing transactions
posts.hook: Monzo ran its core banking ledger on one Cassandra cluster — 21 nodes, replication factor 3, quorum reads. On July 29th, 2019, they scaled it the way they always did: added 6 more servers. Forty-some minutes later, customers' account balances were showing the wrong numbers.
posts.key_numbers: 21-node Cassandra cluster, RF3, local quorum reads → +6 servers at ~13:10 on July 29, 2019 → wrong balances within ~40 minutes → ~1 hour from first alert to confirming Cassandra as the cause → fully resolved in ~90 minutes, nodes decommissioned one at a time at ~8-10 min each.
posts.lesson: Nobody set auto_bootstrap wrong on purpose. It's the kind of assumption that's correct right up until the day it's tested for real, on a live system, with customers' money running through it.

posts.topic: Rejected the microservices + cloud-autoscaling default and ran the entire Q&A network on a monolith across 9 on-premise web servers, individually specced hardware (Dell R630 web tier, NVMe-backed SQL clusters with 384-768GB RAM, dedicated Redis and Elasticsearch tiers) instead of scaling out horizontally
posts.hook: On February 9th, 2016, Stack Overflow's engineers published exactly what their infrastructure looked like — nine web servers, one monolith, on-premise hardware — and it broke every rule of the standard 'break the monolith, move to the cloud, scale out horizontally' playbook.
posts.key_numbers: Feb 9, 2016 (one day, 9 web servers): 209.4M HTTP requests, 66.3M page loads, 504.8M SQL queries, 5.8B Redis hits, 17.2M Elasticsearch searches. Question page render: 22.71ms avg server-side. SQL server CPU: 5-10% almost always. Redis: ~160B ops/month at <2% CPU per instance. Hardware: Dell R630 web tier (dual 12-core Xeons, 64GB RAM); SQL clusters at 384GB and 768GB RAM over NVMe; 4 HAProxy load balancers.
posts.lesson: Microservices and cloud autoscaling are the default because they solve real problems — team autonomy, isolated deploys, bursty load. Stack Overflow didn't have those problems. It had predictable traffic and engineers who measured the ceiling before building anything to raise it. The industry's default architecture isn't wrong — it's just routinely applied to bottlenecks nobody bothered to check for.

posts.topic: Gorilla in-memory time series database — 26-hour write-through cache in front of HBase, delta-of-delta timestamp encoding + XOR float compression bringing 16-byte points down to 1.37 bytes average
posts.hook: The slowest query Facebook's monitoring system served was the one an on-call engineer ran mid-incident — so they built a database whose entire trick was fitting 26 hours of every metric on the fleet into RAM
posts.key_numbers: 16 bytes raw/point → 1.37 bytes avg (~12x compression). ~73x lower query latency, ~14x higher throughput vs HBase. ODS: ~450 qps at launch → Gorilla 5,000+ steady-state qps, peaks past 40,000. 26-hour in-memory retention window. Prolonged outage: keeps ~1 minute of data, drops the rest. Beringei open-sourced 2017, archived 2018.
posts.lesson: The architecture wasn't the trick — fitting a full day of every metric on the fleet into RAM was. The compression scheme mirrors the shape of the signal it compresses: fixed interval, barely changing, read as a recent range.

posts.topic: Kafka-buffered Elasticsearch ingestion — an Ingestion Service queues client writes into one Kafka topic per Elasticsearch cluster, drained by a bounded worker pool, after direct writes into a bounded ES write thread pool caused total index/cluster loss under traffic spikes
posts.hook: It's a breaking-news night, and somewhere inside Twitter's search infrastructure a queue tied to a thread pool is filling faster than it drains. Minutes later the cluster isn't slow. It's gone.
posts.key_numbers: Not independently verified with hard node/QPS/latency figures from the primary source (post focuses on architecture, not those metrics). Backfill Service operations described as often spanning several, sometimes hundreds of terabytes of data.
posts.lesson: The tradeoffs didn't disappear. They moved — from a database that falls over loudly to a queue that falls behind quietly.

posts.topic: Cache smearing — Ketama consistent hashing let Etsy resize memcached pools for years without a mass rehash, until one hot key's own GET traffic alone saturated a single host's NIC; adding more hosts didn't help because consistent hashing guarantees that key always lands on exactly one host, so the fix was appending random entropy to the key on every read/write, splitting one logical key into up to 16 physical keys spread across the pool
posts.hook: One key. On a memcached pool spread across dozens of hosts, a single hot key pushed one box's network interface to 960 megabits a second — on a 1 gigabit card.
posts.key_numbers: Outbound > 800Mbps: p90 GET latency 5ms → 35ms. NIC saturates near 960Mbps on a 1Gbps card: latency > 200ms. Smearing entropy range: 0-8, sometimes 0-16 (up to 16 physical keys per hot key).
posts.lesson: Consistent hashing's whole guarantee is one key maps to one host, deterministically, at any pool size — exactly what makes horizontal scaling free for ordinary keys, and exactly why it's powerless against one key that's hot enough on its own.

posts.topic: H3 hexagonal hierarchical spatial index — pre-H3 surge pricing ran on geofenced zones, producing an "edge effect" where riders meters apart across a zone boundary paid very different multipliers and drivers idled inside high-price zones; squares can't fix this even at finer resolution because they have two neighbor distances (edge d vs. corner d×√2), while a hexagon's 6 neighbors all share an edge at one distance — the exact uniformity a price-smoothing gradient needs — at the cost of exactly 12 topologically mandatory pentagon cells (5 neighbors) at every resolution, which Uber orients into open ocean via the icosahedron's placement
posts.hook: Every mapping tool you've ever used defaults to squares. Pixels are squares. Lat/lon grids are squares. Spreadsheets are squares. Uber's surge-pricing team looked at that default and threw it out — they rebuilt the map out of hexagons.
posts.key_numbers: 16 H3 resolutions; average edge length ~1,107.71km at res 0 down to ~0.51m at res 15; res 8 (~461m edge, ~0.5km² per cell) is the resolution surge pricing commonly runs at; square neighbor distance ratio d×1.41 (corner) vs. d (edge); resolution 0 has exactly 122 base cells (110 hexagons + 12 pentagons).
posts.lesson: Surge pricing needs to interpolate a continuous value across discrete cells — a gradient, not a lookup table — which only works if every neighbor is the same distance away; H3 doesn't make pricing smoother by being cleverer about zones, it changes the shape of space so smoothing becomes arithmetic, at the cost of 12 topologically unavoidable pentagons Uber has to hide in the ocean.

posts.topic: Postgres scaling — a single primary on AWS's largest instance hit reliability problems from autovacuum on multi-terabyte tables, so Figma moved whole tables to their own databases (vertical partitioning) via a logical-replication cutover that dropped and rebuilt indexes to survive terabyte-scale copies, then validated a view-based logical sharding layer with 100% shadow reads before building DBProxy, a Go query proxy that parses SQL to an AST and routes by shard key
posts.hook: Figma's database stack grew almost 100x between 2020 and 2024. In 2020: one Postgres primary, already on AWS's largest physical instance. By end of 2022: a dozen separate databases. By September 2023: parts of it finally sharded. Nobody just "added shards" — the path between those points is the interesting part.
posts.key_numbers: 2020: 1 primary on AWS's largest instance. End of 2022: a dozen vertically partitioned databases. Database stack grew ~100x, 2020-2024. Logical replication cutover reduced to hours by dropping/rebuilding indexes. Shadow-read overhead: minimal typical, <10% worst case. First sharded tables live September 2023.
posts.lesson: The real ceiling wasn't table size, it was that Postgres autovacuum's cost scales with table size (MVCC dead tuples + transaction ID freezing), so the maintenance operation that keeps the database correct stopped fitting inside the traffic pattern; sharding wasn't one decision but a sequence of smaller, reversible ones, each validated before the next became load-bearing.

posts.topic: January 4th 2021 Transit Gateway outage - cold-cache reconnect storm saturated a shared AWS Transit Gateway, packet loss made CPU-based autoscaling read the incident as idle capacity and scale the web tier down, then the autoscaler's overcorrection (1,200 servers requested in 15 minutes) drove provision-service into a Linux open-file-descriptor limit
posts.hook: 6:57am PST: Slack's message-send success rate reads 99%. Normal is above 99.999% - a thousand-fold jump in failures, and the incident is just getting started.
posts.key_numbers: 6:57am PST message-send success rate ~99% vs normal >99.999%. 7:01-7:15am PST: 1,200 servers requested at once. Provisioning hit a Linux open-file-descriptor limit. ~90 min fully unusable, ~8:15am PST provision-service recovers.
posts.lesson: CPU utilization is a fine proxy for load only when compute is what's actually saturated - under network I/O wait it inverts, reading idle exactly when the service is most saturated, which is why the autoscaler scaled down mid-incident before overcorrecting into a second, un-load-tested limit.

posts.topic: Annoy approximate nearest-neighbor search — random-projection forest of trees for music-recommendation vectors, plus mmap'd read-only index files so many worker processes share one physical copy instead of duplicating it per process
posts.hook: Erik Bernhardsson built Annoy at Spotify in a couple of afternoons during a Hack Week in 2013 — and thirteen years later it's still doing the job it was hacked together for
posts.key_numbers: 5,000,000 items × 40 floats × 4 bytes = 800MB (Annoy's own illustrative math). × 32 worker processes with private copies = 25.6GB vs. 800MB flat when mmap'd and shared. search_k defaults to n_trees × n. Built 2013, in a couple of afternoons during a Hack Week.
posts.lesson: The same random-projection trick that makes the search approximate is what makes the index a flat, pointer-free, read-only file — exactly the shape mmap needs to back every worker process with one physical copy instead of many.

posts.topic: Why a 3-engineer team never split the Django app into microservices — a stateless app tier scales by cloning the process, while the genuinely hard sharding/replication/consistency problems were pushed one layer down into Postgres, Redis, and Memcached
posts.hook: Instagram hit 14 million users in about 14 months with 3 backend engineers, and never broke up the monolith — not then, not at 300 million users, not in 2024 when Meta shipped Threads off the same codebase in five months
posts.key_numbers: 3 backend engineers, 14M users in ~14 months. App tier: 3 nginx + 25+ stateless Django/Gunicorn instances behind an ELB. Data tier: 12 large Postgres instances, Redis holding a ~300M photo-to-user-ID map in ~5GB, 6 Memcached nodes. By 2019: several million lines of Python, a few thousand Django endpoints, ~100 custom lint rules, ~100 deploys/day. 2024: Threads shipped off the same monolith in 5 months.
posts.lesson: Statelessness is the specific property that makes horizontal cloning of a monolith nearly free — the problem was request/data volume, not code complexity needing independent ownership, so the real hard distributed-systems work (sharding, replication, consistency) got pushed into the data tier instead of spread across a service mesh.

posts.topic: Quicksilver config-distribution store — replaced single-root Kyoto Tycoon with per-server LMDB (memory-mapped B+tree, single-writer/multi-reader MVCC) and a hash-chained async replication tree, then split into replica/proxy roles in 2025 as the dataset outgrew small colocations
posts.hook: One physical root server for every config change on Cloudflare's edge. Faulty hardware made it disappear, so they rebuilt config distribution around a memory-mapped database on every single box instead.
posts.key_numbers: 5B+ key-value pairs, 1.6TB total, 3B+ keys/sec served worldwide, 90% of requests <1ms, 99.9% <7ms. DNS/rule changes reach 90% of the fleet in seconds. Kyoto Tycoon removal took ~4 years across 50+ producer teams. PIPEFAIL incident: Dec 16 2021, 20:10-20:40 UTC, up to 5s added latency for 30 minutes.
posts.lesson: The exact mechanism that makes global replication fast — near-instant fan-out of tiny deltas to every server — is the same mechanism that turns one bad write into a global incident just as fast.

posts.company: Redis / Redis community (antirez vs. Martin Kleppmann)
posts.topic: The 2016 Redlock debate — Redis's quorum-based distributed lock (5 independent masters, majority acquisition, elapsed-time TTL check) versus Kleppmann's fencing-token critique of what happens after a client wins the lock and then stalls
posts.hook: In February 2016, Redis's creator and a Cambridge database researcher spent two weeks publicly disagreeing about whether a lock actually locks anything.
posts.key_numbers: Redlock: 5 independent Redis masters, no replication between them, majority = 3/5, canonical 10s TTL, clock drift margin ~1% of TTL + a couple ms. Worked failure case: Client 1 acquires lock, hits a ~30s GC pause, lease expires at T+10s, Client 2 acquires at T+10.2s and writes, Client 1 wakes at T+30s unaware and writes too — no fencing token to distinguish the writes.
posts.lesson: Redlock's quorum solves the failure mode of a crashed or failed-over node forging a second lock grant; it does not and cannot solve a live client that pauses past its own lease, because the lock itself is a yes/no with no monotonically increasing token — that gap only closes if the protected resource enforces a fencing check itself.

posts.topic: Why Uber Engineering switched from Postgres to MySQL in 2016 — physical index write amplification, autovacuum full-table scans, and a Postgres 9.2 replication-corruption incident that forced hand resyncing every replica
posts.hook: Postgres indexes point straight at a row's physical location on disk. MySQL's InnoDB indexes point at the primary key instead — one extra hop. That single architectural difference is most of the reason Uber ripped Postgres out, ten years ago this week.
posts.key_numbers: Published July 26, 2016, exactly ten years before this post. Postgres secondary indexes point at a row's physical heap offset (every column update rewrites every index on the row); MySQL/InnoDB secondary indexes point at the primary key (one extra lookup hop, only the clustered index moves on a row relocation). A Postgres 9.2 bug during a routine upgrade corrupted index pages on a handful of rows per database; because Postgres replication is physical (page-level WAL), the corruption replayed onto every standby while the newly promoted master stayed clean, forcing a full manual resync of every replica from a fresh snapshot. Uber had already run out of room on its Postgres trip tables by early 2014 and had Schemaless (append-only, sharded, on plain MySQL) live in production by October 2014.
posts.lesson: Postgres wasn't the wrong database in 2011 — it was the wrong database for the write pattern and scale Uber grew into by 2015. A row-store's physical-index design is a real, specific cost (write amplification, vacuum scans, replication fragility under corruption) that only shows up once you're pushing enough writes through it, and by then the fix is architectural, not a config tweak.

posts.topic: KIP-500 removed Kafka's ZooKeeper dependency — full-metadata-tree reloads on controller failover and one-shot-watch RPC fan-out were replaced by a self-managed Raft metadata quorum (KRaft), cutting failover from 20+ minutes to under a second
posts.hook: For a decade, the fix for a slow Kafka controller failover was "give ZooKeeper more headroom." That was never going to work.
posts.key_numbers: On controller failover, the ZooKeeper-based controller had to reload the entire metadata tree (every topic, partition, replica assignment, ISR) into memory before issuing any LeaderAndIsr directives — an O(total partitions) reload that KIP-500's own motivation cites as stretching past 20 minutes on large clusters, capping practical cluster size around roughly 200,000 partitions. ZooKeeper watches are one-shot (fire once, must be re-registered), and the controller's own metadata propagation used full-state UpdateMetadataRequest RPCs to every broker on every change. KIP-500 (proposed 2019) replaced this with an embedded Raft quorum over a __cluster_metadata log; standby controllers are Raft followers already replaying that log, so failover became a leader vote instead of a data-load — typically under a second. KIP-833 marked KRaft production-ready in Kafka 3.3 (October 3, 2022). KAFKA-6879 is a real filed bug: a ZooKeeper session expiration could deadlock the controller's own internal lock against its own expiry-handling latch, leaving a silent "zombie" controller that never issued another directive until manually restarted.
posts.lesson: For a decade the instinct was to tune ZooKeeper harder because it was the proven, boring default embedded across HBase, Solr, and Kafka itself. But the bottleneck was never ZooKeeper's throughput — it was that an external, session-based coordination service forces a full-state reload on every failover, no matter how well-provisioned the ensemble is. Sometimes the slow thing isn't slow because it needs tuning; it's slow because your control plane's source of truth lives in somebody else's system.

posts.topic: Zuul's two rewrites — the 2017 move from thread-per-connection (Zuul 1, Servlet) to a Netty event-loop architecture (Zuul 2) to fix thread-pool exhaustion under retry storms, and the 2023 fix for the connection-count explosion that the event-loop rewrite introduced
posts.hook: Every reverse proxy has the same nightmare: a backend gets slow, and the thing meant to protect you from it runs out of capacity right along with it.
posts.key_numbers: Zuul 1 (2013): one thread per connection (Servlet model); backend slowdowns held threads longer while retries added connections, exhausting the thread pool. Zuul 2 (2017, Netty, non-blocking): one event loop per CPU core, Linux epoll (edge-triggered) underneath, separate outbound connection pool per host per event loop. Measured after months in production, not uniform: +25% throughput / -25% CPU on the I/O-bound logging-pipeline cluster (write-heavy, large requests, small responses), 0% gain on the CPU-bound API cluster (metrics, encryption, compression done per request). By 2018, 80+ Zuul 2 clusters routing to ~100 backend service clusters, 1M+ requests/second aggregate. 2023 fix (HTTP/2 multiplexing + host subsetting) cut peak connections by ~10x across all 3 AWS regions, with some shards reduced by up to 13 million connections at peak.
posts.lesson: The primitive that scales with your traffic is whatever quantity you multiply requests by. Thread-per-connection multiplies by concurrent slow waits; an event loop fixes that by holding pending state as callback data on a fixed thread count instead of blocking an OS thread per wait. But the fix didn't remove the multiplication, it moved it — from threads to connections (instances x event loops x backend hosts) — which is why the same gateway needed a second, unrelated rewrite six years later.

posts.topic: The sync engine — treating each browser tab as a Postgres-style logical replica: a global monotonically increasing sync id (client-side LSN) driving ordered delta-packet broadcast over WebSocket, IndexedDB as the local replica, and lazy per-view hydration of unbounded tables to keep bootstrap cost tied to workspace structure rather than workspace size
posts.hook: Every field you edit in Linear writes to your browser's IndexedDB before a single byte reaches the server.
posts.key_numbers: Single global lastSyncId counter incremented once per accepted mutation across the whole system; each mutation emits a delta packet (Insert/Update/Archive/Delete/etc.) tagged with that id, broadcast to every connected client including the originator. Bootstrap fetches a full snapshot at a known sync id then streams deltas forward, mirroring snapshot + streaming-WAL logical replication. Issues and comments (the two unbounded tables) lazy-hydrate per view via partial indexes; bounded workspace metadata (labels, states, projects) still bootstraps eagerly. Result: a 10,000-issue workspace boots in about the same time as a 100-issue one.
posts.lesson: Nobody CRDT'd their way out of merge conflicts here. They noticed the problem was never reconciling concurrent edits, it was keeping a replica caught up — and reached for the same log-tailing idea Postgres has used for decades, one browser tab at a time.

posts.topic: f4, Facebook's warm BLOB storage system — decoupling durability from throughput by replacing Haystack's uniform 3.6x triple replication with Reed-Solomon(10,4) erasure coding (1.4x local overhead) plus cross-datacenter XOR coding (2.1x effective), routed by a trailing 99th-percentile IOPS/TB signal per volume
posts.hook: By 2014, Facebook was storing over 65 petabytes in Haystack, and every byte — ten seconds old or four years old — was replicated 3.6 times.
posts.key_numbers: 65PB+ logical BLOBs stored by f4 at publication. Haystack replication factor: 3x geographic x 1.2 RAID-6 = 3.6x. For 8 of 9 BLOB types, week-old content saw an order-of-magnitude fewer reads than day-old content. Migration trigger: 99th-percentile IOPS/TB below 20 (a 4TB drive safely serves ~80 IOPS). Photos migrate to f4 at 3 months, other types at 1 month; profile photos never migrate. f4 mechanism: Reed-Solomon(10,4) = 1.4x single-DC overhead, geo-mirrored to 2.8x, XOR-coded across datacenters down to 2.1x effective replication factor, still tolerant of a full datacenter loss.
posts.lesson: Haystack wasn't a bad design, it was tuned for 2008's corpus where almost everything was recently uploaded. The real problem was that one replication number was answering two different questions -- durability and throughput -- for six years after the corpus's shape had already changed underneath it.

posts.topic: Spanner's TrueTime — bounding physical clock uncertainty to single-digit milliseconds with GPS + atomic-clock time masters and Marzullo's algorithm, then explicitly waiting out that bound (commit-wait) to get external consistency across causally unrelated transactions, instead of falling back to logical clocks
posts.hook: Every distributed-systems text says the same thing: never trust wall-clock time. Google built Spanner by trusting it more than anyone ever had.
posts.key_numbers: TrueTime API returns TTinterval = [earliest, latest] instead of a point timestamp. Epsilon (ε) follows a sawtooth: time masters (GPS-based, plus a minority of pure-atomic-clock 'Armageddon masters') are polled every 30s; assuming a worst-case drift rate of ~200μs/s, ε swings from ~1ms right after a sync to ~7ms right before the next, combined via Marzullo's algorithm across multiple noisy references. Commit-wait holds a transaction's result until TT.now().earliest is provably past its commit timestamp s — typically a few ms, bounded by ε rather than round-trip time. External consistency: if T2 starts after T1 commits in real time, T2's commit timestamp is guaranteed greater than T1's, even with zero causal link between them — a guarantee logical clocks (Lamport, vector) cannot make since they only order communicating events.
posts.lesson: "Avoid physical time" is the industry default because it's the cheap way out — Spanner instead priced the hard problem honestly, in racks of GPS receivers and atomic clocks, and found it cheaper than living without a global commit order. The same hardware dependency is why nobody outside Google adopts TrueTime directly; CockroachDB built Hybrid Logical Clocks instead, trading a tighter real-time bound for commodity hardware and more transaction retries under clock skew.

posts.topic: rpcmap — deriving Calico NetworkPolicy for 1,500+ microservices from static analysis of the actual Go RPC-client call graph instead of a hand-maintained policy document, then staging default-deny enforcement (alerts-only, then logging, then +1 month with drops still off) specifically to surface rarely-triggered, including yearly, code paths before going live
posts.hook: Monzo made an unusual call for a bank running 1,500 microservices: deny every connection between services by default, and only reopen the paths a machine could prove were real.
posts.key_numbers: ~1,500 services with 9,300+ live service-to-service calls on a flat Kubernetes network (2019). rpcmap statically derives the RPC call graph from Go source; Calico NetworkPolicy is generated from that graph as default-deny + pod-label allow-lists (not IPs). Rollout: alerts-only for weeks, then logging (sized via calico-accountant), then drops held off a further month to catch yearly-cadence code paths, before enforcement. Fleet later grew to 2,100+ services with Prometheus-driven automated rollback (2022) and 2,800 services with a dedicated migrations team and config-driven gradual rollout (2024).
posts.lesson: Past a few hundred services, any process that assumes a human is keeping two systems in sync — a policy doc and the code, a dashboard and a live deploy, a migration and every service owner's calendar — is already lying to you. The fix isn't better documentation, it's generating the documentation from the thing it describes.

posts.topic: Entity Cache — moving service-to-service caching out of each microservice process and into the Envoy-based service mesh (backed by Valkey), so concurrent cache misses for the same entity coalesce via a single-flight lock instead of each pod independently hammering the upstream
posts.hook: A hundred pods once watched the same cache entry expire within the same second — and all hundred independently called the same upstream service to refetch it.
posts.key_numbers: Entity Cache serves 1.5M+ requests/sec across 100+ endpoints and 50 services, 90%+ cache hit rate on the busiest endpoints, 99.99999% availability. Optimizations (custom buffer pools, lock-free single-flight, XFetch probabilistic early refresh) cut allocation rates 50-60%, raised per-pod throughput ~5x, and cut P99 latency spikes by up to 80%. Invalidation is Kafka-event-driven, comparing update timestamps instead of pushing distributed deletes.
posts.lesson: No one was wrong. Per-service caching does cut a process's own repeat calls — it just can't see what every other pod is asking for at the same instant. The tradeoff didn't disappear when DoorDash moved caching into the mesh. It moved to whoever forgets to publish a Kafka event.
